games.title: Name the type
games.instructions: Match each expression to the type Python gives it.

pairs.explanation: A whole number with no decimal point is an int.
A decimal point makes it a float.
Quotes make it a string, even when it looks like a number.
Square brackets make a list.
The trailing comma is what makes (7,) a tuple; (7) is just 7.
True and False are the two bool values.

games.title: Can it change?
games.instructions: Sort each value by whether it can be changed in place.

items.explanation: Lists are mutable: nums[0] = 9 works.
Dictionaries are mutable: you can add and replace keys.
Sets are mutable: add() and remove() change them.
Strings are immutable: name[5] = 'X' raises a TypeError.
Tuples are immutable once made.
Numbers are immutable; x = x + 1 makes a new number.

games.title: Output pairs
games.instructions: Flip two tiles at a time to find each piece of code and its output.

pairs.explanation: None is still an item, so the list has four.
// divides and rounds down to a whole number.
** raises to a power: 2 × 2 × 2.
Multiplying a string repeats it.
+ joins strings with nothing in between.

pairs.a:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a)
pairs.explanation: a, b = b, a swaps the two values.

games.title: Ranges and slices
games.instructions: Match each expression to its value.

pairs.explanation: range stops one before the end value.
Starts at 8 and stops before 10.
The third value is the step.
A set keeps one of each value: {1, 2, 3}.
Characters 6 and 7; the slice stops before 8.

games.title: Sort by type
games.instructions: Put each expression under the type of value it produces.

items.explanation: // on two ints gives an int: 3.
len always returns an int.
/ always gives a float in Python 3: 3.5.
// with a float involved gives a float: 2.0.
A fractional power gives a float.
Repeating a string gives a string: "77".
str() turns a value into text.
Repeating a list gives a list: [1, 1, 1].
list() on a string splits it into characters.

games.title: Loop outputs
games.instructions: Find each loop and what it prints.

pairs.a:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(i, end=" ")
pairs.explanation: range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3.
A for loop over a string visits each character.
A negative step counts down.
5, 6, 7, 8 and 9: five numbers.
+ joins two lists into one.
max returns the largest item.

games.title: What does it return?
games.instructions: Match each function call to the value it returns.

pairs.explanation: b was not given, so it takes its default of 10.
*nums gathers every argument into a tuple.
A function with no return statement returns None.
str(7) is "7", then "!" is joined on.
A lambda is a one-line function: 5 ** 2.

games.title: Error or fine?
games.instructions: Sort each line by whether it runs or raises an error.

items.explanation: index raises ValueError when the item is not in the list.
A missing key raises KeyError.
int only reads digits: ValueError.
Index 5 is past the end: IndexError.
Tuples cannot be changed: TypeError.
"12" is all digits, so it becomes 12.
Slices past the end are allowed; this gives "bc".
get returns None for a missing key instead of raising.

games.title: Dictionaries and scope
games.instructions: Find each piece of code and what it prints.

pairs.explanation: len counts the keys.
get returns the default when the key is missing.
keys() gives the keys in the order they were added.
104 and 105 are the character codes for h and i.

pairs.a:
counter = 1
def add():
    global counter
    counter += 3
add()
print(counter)
pairs.explanation: global lets the function change the outer counter.
join puts the string between each item.

games.title: Commands and what they do
games.instructions: Match each IPython command to what it does.

pairs.explanation: linspace(start, stop, count) includes both ends.

pairs.right: Saves the plot as an image
pairs.explanation: The file goes in the current working directory.
Calling it again replaces the label.
"o" is the circle marker.
Same shape as the input, filled with ones.

pairs.right: Reads numbers from a text file
pairs.explanation: Every row needs the same number of values.

games.title: True or false?
games.instructions: Sort each statement into true or false.

items.text: Indentation is part of Python's syntax
items.explanation: The indentation marks where a block starts and ends.

items.text: "in" works on lists, tuples, strings and dicts
items.explanation: For a dict, in checks the keys.
/ is true division; // is floor division.

items.text: The first item in a list is at index 1
items.explanation: Python counts from 0.
range(5) is 0 to 4.
Any consistent indentation works; 4 spaces is the convention.
